$comment: Hand-maintained. There is no generator and no --write flag, and that is deliberate.
The dependency baseline is a ratchet you regenerate with one command, because those
findings are debt being paid down. This file is not that. A secret is either a false
positive or an incident, and a --write flag here would let a real leak be accepted
with one command. Every entry is added by hand and needs a reason a reviewer can check.
Entries key on path plus a SHA-256 prefix of the matched text, never the text itself,
so accepting a finding never writes the string back into the repository. The id is
printed by `npm run lint:secrets` next to each finding. Note that a hash only conceals
a high-entropy value, and a real credential should be rotated rather than recorded
here anyway. Moving an accepted string to a new file fails until that path is added,
which is the point: the set of hardcoded key literals cannot grow unreviewed.
Two groups below, and only two.
1. The demo stack's bootstrap key, id 4ce0f9725485398b, plus the key_prefix column
value derived from it, id 1f9725a8294b349c. `docker compose --profile demo up
--build` is the
headline command in the README, and it seeds an api_keys row with tenant_id NULL
and scopes {read,write,admin}: a global admin grant whose plaintext is committed.
This is allowlisted rather than flagged. It is not a credential to anything real:
it exists only in a database the same commit creates, it cannot be rotated because
there is nothing to rotate it at, and it is published in the README, docker-compose
and the seed script by design. Flagging it would fail the check on every run
forever, and a check that always fails is a check everyone bypasses.
What the allowlist buys instead is pinning: these seven occurrences are the whole
known-good set, so changing the key, or using it in an eighth file, fails.
Migration 011 already removed this key from the schema migrations for exactly this
reason. The remaining exposure is a demo stack reachable from a network, which is
a deployment concern tracked separately, not a secret-scanning one.
2. Truncated key examples in the docs site and one Storybook fixture: elided stand-ins
that illustrate the shape of a key_prefix, a plaintext_key and a sensitive config
value. They are too short to be minted keys and are not placeholder-shaped, so the
rule cannot tell them apart from a real short literal without a human saying so.
Note that this file names no key text anywhere, including in these comments. That is
the rule it exists to enforce, so writing an example here would fail the check, which
is how it should be.
